Posteriormente, señaló que había interceptado 10 misiles balísticos disparados hacia el sur de Arabia Saudita. Los hutíes advirtieron que podrían volver a atacar el Aeropuerto Internacional Rey Khalid de Riad, que reanudó el domingo sus operaciones en dos terminales tras una incursión a principios de este mes. Los hutíes afirmaron que el sábado atacaron el aeropuerto e instalaciones petroleras sauditas. Riad no se pronunció directamente sobre las declaraciones de los hutíes. El portavoz militar hutí, Yahya Saree, afirmó que el aeropuerto seguía siendo un "objetivo militar" y advirtió a todas las aerolíneas, al personal del aeropuerto y a los viajeros que no lo utilizaran. El aeropuerto suspendió sus operaciones el 10 de octubre tras un ataque —reivindicado por los hutíes— que causó la muerte de 13 personas y dejó más de 300 heridos, el más mortífero en el reino en una década. Riad intensificó sus ataques contra los hutíes después de que el grupo se hiciera con el control de territorio estratégico a lo largo de la costa del mar Rojo, acercándose al estrecho de Bab el-Mandeb —un punto estratégico marítimo mundial y ruta de transporte para los productores de petróleo del Golfo, en el lado opuesto de la península arábiga al estrecho de Ormuz-. La reanudación de los combates en Yemen ha hecho añicos una tregua negociada por la ONU que se había mantenido en gran medida desde 2022. Arabia Saudita intervino en la guerra civil de Yemen en 2015 al frente de una coalición que apoyaba al Gobierno reconocido internacionalmente, después de que los hutíes tomaran la capital, Saná, un año antes.

item.title: French protest groups demand more rallies as Macron faces tough choices
item.description: The government began talks with unions and student representatives to defuse the crisis, but protest leaders say the measures it has proposed are inadequate.
item.dc:creator: Crispian Balmer, Juliette Jabkhiro
item.content:encoded: French protest groups and unions called on Sunday for further demonstrations as they sought to maintain pressure on the government after a huge security operation helped to contain unrest during nationwide rallies on Saturday. The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in Saturday's marches as authorities deployed 70,000 police, helping to avert a repeat of the looting and vandalism that swept many cities on October 17. Labour leaders urged further protests next Saturday and a nationwide strike on November 5, saying frustration over wages, living costs and public services was spreading far beyond the student movement that first mobilised last month. "We see an aggregation of anger," Murielle Guilbert, co-leader of the left-wing Solidaires trade union federation, told BFM TV. She said grievances from students, workers, firefighters and other groups were converging. "We call on people to take to the streets next Saturday." The SUD Education teaching union said it would join the October 31 demonstration while the large CGT union said it would decide during the week. MACRON'S SCOPE TO RESPOND IS MINIMAL The Yellow Vests, a grassroots movement that emerged in 2018 as a revolt against fuel taxes, also called for mass rallies next Saturday, including sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly. "There is anger in this country. It's growing in schools and universities, on roundabouts, in neighbourhoods, on farms and in workplaces," activist Azelma Sigaux told reporters. In 2019, President Emmanuel Macron was able to find the resources to reduce fuel costs in response to the Yellow Vests. Seven years on, strained public finances leave him with little room to meet protesters' demands. His mandate also expires next April and his centrist party no longer has the majority needed to pass major legislation. The government has begun talks with unions and student representatives to try to defuse the crisis, but protest leaders say the measures it has proposed so far are inadequate. "We have received no response at all from this government," said Guilbert. Police unions said on Sunday they did not have enough staff to maintain for any length of time the high level of deployment that on Saturday helped to limit disorder to sporadic clashes in a number of cities, including Paris and Marseille. Some 1,314 people were arrested on Saturday, half of last week's numbers, the interior ministry said on Sunday, and about 50 police were injured, compared with more than 1,000 last week. The protests have resonated beyond France's borders. On Saturday [USN:L6N46A05C TEXT:"Belgian police"] used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators. [USN:FWN4630JL TEXT:"In Albania"], peaceful protests that began at the end of May this month turned into violent unrest and skirmishes have taken place in several Italian cities for a second week running.

item.title: Anderson disappointed to see 25-year Lancashire journey come to an end
item.description: Fast bowler James Anderson expressed disappointment on Sunday after Lancashire decided not to renew his contract, bringing an end to a 25-year association between England's all-time leading test wicket-taker and his home county.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Fast bowler James Anderson expressed disappointment on Sunday after Lancashire decided not to renew his contract, bringing an end to a 25-year association between England's all-time leading test wicket-taker and his home county. Anderson, who claimed 704 test wickets for England, will leave Lancashire as the county look to move on from the 44-year-old and rebuild their squad for a promotion push from Division Two of the County Championship. The veteran bowler made 112 first-class appearances for Lancashire, claiming 443 wickets, and was involved in their County Championship title triumph in 2011. "I've supported Lancashire since I was a kid, and so to get to play for them for 25 years was a dream come true," Anderson said in a statement. "I have always found it special walking out to play at Old Trafford and have some incredible memories of doing so including the honour of being captain. "If it was up to me it wouldn't have ended like this but I wish the players and fans all the best for the future." Anderson, who was appointed Lancashire's red-ball captain for the first time in his career in the 2026 season, took 50 wickets at an average of 17.68 this summer, but the county finished seventh out of eight teams in the second division. "I spoke to Jimmy about our ambitions to rebuild our men's squad that is capable of securing promotion from Division Two of the County Championship and then challenging to win Division One over the next three to four years," said Paul Farbrace, Lancashire's incoming director of cricket. "We are keen to begin that rebuild now, both in terms of the playing squad and the wider professional cricket set-up, and to make important progress over the coming months. "As part of those plans, I informed Jimmy that we had taken the incredibly difficult decision not to extend his playing contract for the 2027 season." Lancashire Cricket had honoured Anderson's contribution to the club by renaming the Pavilion End at Old Trafford the James Anderson End. He was also knighted in 2025 in recognition of his services to cricket.

item.title: Grupo trabajadores advierte de importantes pérdidas de puestos de trabajo en Suiza si UBS se traslada
item.description: Hasta 12.000 puestos de trabajo de UBS en Suiza podrían verse amenazados si unas normas de capital más estrictas obligaran al banco a trasladarse, dijo la Asociación Suiza de Empleados Bancarios (SBPV).
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Hasta 12.000 puestos de trabajo de UBS (UBSG.S) en Suiza podrían verse amenazados si unas normas de capital más estrictas obligaran al banco a trasladarse, dijo la Asociación Suiza de Empleados Bancarios (SBPV). En una carta dirigida a los legisladores y publicada por primera vez el fin de semana por el periódico NZZ am Sonntag, la asociación advirtió que una relocalización, venta o fusión de UBS podría suponer la pérdida de entre 10.000 y 12.000 de los aproximadamente 34.000 puestos de trabajo de UBS en Suiza. La carta, a la que también tuvo acceso Reuters, describía esta situación como el "peor de los casos" y se suma a los recortes ya realizados en el banco mientras completa la integración de Credit Suisse, que adquirió en 2023. UBS, que ha afirmado en repetidas ocasiones que quiere permanecer en Suiza, se negó a comentar la estimación de la SBPV. Un portavoz de UBS afirmó que el banco mantendría al mínimo posible los recortes de empleo derivados de la adquisición de Credit Suisse. UBS ha señalado que sigue previendo unos 3.000 despidos en Suiza como consecuencia de la integración y que estos se producirían a lo largo de varios años, principalmente a través de medidas como la rotación natural de personal, las jubilaciones anticipadas y la internalización de puestos de trabajo que antes se realizaban de forma externa. La advertencia de la SBPV se produce mientras una comisión de la cámara baja del Parlamento suizo se dispone a debatir cuánto capital debería mantener UBS para respaldar a sus filiales extranjeras. El mes pasado, la cámara alta propuso que UBS respaldara esas unidades con un 90% de capital ordinario de nivel 1 (CET1). UBS ha sugerido que esa cifra es excesiva y el presidente del banco ha advertido que tendría que plantearse cuidadosamente su futuro en Suiza si las normas resultaran demasiado estrictas. Algunos accionistas han pedido que UBS abandone Suiza, y el banco ha estado elaborando posibles planes de contingencia, entre los que se incluyen el traslado de su sede o la fusión con otra entidad crediticia, dijeron fuentes a Reuters.

item.title: Viceprimer ministro dice Rusia está dispuesta a suministrar a EEUU cualquier cantidad de diesel: TV estatal
item.description: El viceprimer ministro ruso, Alexander Novak, afirmó que Rusia está dispuesta a suministrar a Estados Unidos cualquier cantidad de gasóleo, informó el domingo el canal de televisión estatal
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: El viceprimer ministro ruso, Alexander Novak, afirmó que Rusia está dispuesta a suministrar a Estados Unidos cualquier cantidad de gasóleo, informó el domingo el canal de televisión estatal Vesti. "Todo lo que nuestros socios quieran (...) del volumen total que vamos a exportar. Podemos suministrarlo todo", afirmó Novak en una entrevista. Novak había declarado el viernes que tres petroleros cargados con gasóleo ruso se dirigían a Norteamérica.

item.title: Flávio Bolsonaro vota no Rio e faz apelo para que eleitores compareçam às urnas
item.description: O candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) votou nesta manhã de domingo em uma escola em Vila Isabel, no Rio de Janeiro, e, em breve declaração à imprensa, fez um apelo aos eleitores para que compareçam às urnas.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: O candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) votou nesta manhã de domingo em uma escola em Vila Isabel, no Rio de Janeiro, e, em breve declaração à imprensa, fez um apelo aos eleitores para que compareçam às urnas. "Faça chuva ou faça sol, bora sair de casa para votar, que o Brasil vai mudar e o Brasil vai vencer", disse o senador. A previsão de chuvas fortes em algumas regiões do país neste domingo tem alimentado a preocupação de aumento da abstenção eleitoral neste segundo turno entre Flávio Bolsonaro e o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). "Chegou a hora da mudança de verdade", afirmou o candidato, ao lado da esposa Fernanda e da mãe, Rogéria, comemorando o que disse ter sido uma campanha "leve" e "limpa" para o segundo turno. "Eu vim com propostas mostrando que a gente tem toda a condição de montar um grande time para reorganizar o Brasil", declarou.

item.title: Brasil acude a las urnas en reñido balotaje presidencial entre Lula y Flávio Bolsonaro
item.description: Los brasileños votaban el domingo en una reñida segunda vuelta electoral que podría inclinar bruscamente a la derecha a la nación más grande de América Latina, acercándola a Estados Unidos como parte de un giro conservador más amplio en toda la región.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Griffin
item.content:encoded: Los brasileños votaban el domingo en una reñida segunda vuelta electoral que podría inclinar bruscamente a la derecha a la nación más grande de América Latina, acercándola a Estados Unidos como parte de un giro conservador más amplio en toda la región. El balotaje enfrenta al presidente izquierdista Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva con el senador derechista Flávio Bolsonaro. El hijo del expresidente Jair Bolsonaro dio la sorpresa a principios de mes al liderar la votación en la primera vuelta en contra de lo que decían las encuestas. Un triunfo de Bolsonaro, de 45 años, prolongaría la ola de victorias de la derecha para los candidatos latinoamericanos afines a Donald Trump, mientras que un cuarto mandato para Lula sería una decepción en Washington, que ha tenido roces con su gobierno en materia de comercio y seguridad. Reuters reveló el sábado una campaña dentro del Departamento de Estado de Trump para ayudar a que los Bolsonaro volvieran al poder. La contienda electoral ha estado marcada por escándalos de corrupción, incertidumbre económica y acusaciones de injerencia estadounidense, algo que Washington niega. También se ha visto influenciada por las repercusiones de la condena de Jair Bolsonaro en 2025 por planear un golpe de Estado en 2022, ante la promesa de Flávio de liberar a su padre si resulta elegido. Trump calificó el caso de "caza de brujas" e impuso un arancel del 50% a Brasil en 2025, en una decisión vinculada explícitamente al juicio de Jair Bolsonaro. Si bien muchas de estas medidas fueron posteriormente suavizadas, el mandatario republicano impuso nuevos aranceles a Brasil este año, alegando prácticas comerciales desleales. Lula ha presentado la cercanía del Gobierno de Trump con el clan Bolsonaro como parte de un intento de influir en las elecciones, al tiempo que ha calificado los aranceles y otras medidas punitivas de intimidación. "No podemos entregar Brasil", afirmó Elenildes dos Reis, una abogada de 60 años de São Paulo que votó por Lula y señaló que su victoria sería una forma de plantarle cara a Trump y a lo que ella describió como una ola creciente de fascismo. "No será solo nuestra victoria, será la del mundo", añadió. En materia económica, a pesar de la disminución de la desigualdad y el desempleo, Lula ha tenido dificultades para ganarse a un electorado que lidia con el alto costo de la vida y las elevadas deudas familiares. La violencia endémica de las pandillas también preocupa a los votantes. RESULTADO INCIERTO Bolsonaro ha intentado sacar provecho de la preocupación por el costo de la vida y también ha prometido mano dura para combatir la delincuencia, comprometiéndose a construir cárceles de máxima seguridad y a aplicar la castración química para los delitos sexuales graves. "Necesitamos un cambio", afirmó José Carlos Jarra, un jubilado de 61 años de São Paulo que trabajó en el sector sanitario y votó a Bolsonaro. Dijo esperar que el senador abordara la seguridad pública y hiciera más por los jubilados, y calificó el salario mínimo de Brasil como "una vergüenza". En Río de Janeiro, Alba Marques, una jubilada de 75 años, afirmó que su voto por Bolsonaro era un voto en contra del Partido de los Trabajadores de Lula, no a favor del senador. "Ya no soporto que, desde hace 40 años, un tipo diga que va a arreglar Brasil. Siempre la misma promesa", afirmó. Al emitir su voto en Río de Janeiro el domingo, Flávio Bolsonaro instó a la gente a acudir a las urnas "con lluvia o con sol". Lula, por su parte, votará en São Bernardo do Campo, cerca de São Paulo. Las encuestas muestran que los candidatos están prácticamente empatados de cara a la segunda vuelta, con recortando distancias en los últimos días. Lula votó en São Bernardo do Campo, cerca de São Paulo, y agradeció a sus seguidores. "Lo que la gente ha hecho por mí estos últimos días es algo que nunca podré devolver", dijo a periodistas. Los precedentes históricos favorecen a Bolsonaro, ya que ningún candidato ha ganado la presidencia tras quedar segundo en la primera vuelta de las elecciones. Bolsonaro obtuvo el 47% de los votos emitidos en la primera vuelta, contra e 45% de Lula. La victoria del senador disparó los mercados brasileños y su moneda ante las expectativas de reformas favorables a las empresas. Su éxito en la primera vuelta se vio reflejado en las elecciones al Congreso de su Partido Liberal y de otros políticos de derecha, lo que podría allanarle el camino legislativo o complicarle la gobernabilidad a Lula.

item.title: Conservative party wins first election in nearly a century in British Columbia
item.description: The opposition Conservative Party won an election in the Canadian province of British Columbia for the first time in nearly 100 years, promising to ramp up liquefied natural gas production, provisional results showed on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The opposition Conservative Party won an election in the Canadian province of British Columbia for the first time in nearly 100 years, promising to ramp up liquefied natural gas production, provisional results showed on Sunday. The result marks an end to nine years of power for the left-of-center New Democrats, who voiced opposition to new oil pipelines and supported a ban on tankers along the province's northern coast The right-leaning Conservatives won 64 of the 93 seats and the New Democrats won 27. It is the first Conservative provincial election win since 1928 The Conservatives pledged to double natural gas production by 2032 and more than triple it by 2035 "I believe in energy... We will cut red tape like it's never been cut before," Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson said in his victory speech Doerkson, who will become the next premier of the province, promised to "supercharge" BC. The province will host a business summit in Vancouver next year The Conservatives promised to end emissions limits, replace the province's carbon tax framework and reach out to energy providers that had left the province's LNG sector since 2018, including ExxonMobil, Chevron and Woodside Polls showed voters were focused on cost-of-living issues, healthcare, and the ongoing trade war with US President Donald Trump New Democrat Premier David Eby had called for a strong mandate to confront Trump's tariff threats

item.title: Netanyahu rebuked for plan to use crypto to bypass economic sanctions
item.description: His comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel.
item.dc:creator: Steven Scheer
item.content:encoded: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces [USN:L8N45Y0MD TEXT:"re-election"] this week, is drawing criticism from economists and political rivals after suggesting Israel could use cryptocurrency to help shield its economy from potential international sanctions. In an interview with Israel's Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel. Last month, Britain, France and Canada said they would [USN:S8N42N05Y TEXT:"block imports"] from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in what was the latest in a series of actions targeting Israel's settlement policy, underscoring its growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies. "There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that." Asked whether he was referring to cryptocurrency, Netanyahu replied: "Very true, very true," adding that blockchain technology was another possibility. The comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel, which said crypto currencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions and that political leaders should focus on policy that would render such measures unnecessary. "The right course for Israel's economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy," it said. Netanyahu on Sunday continued to defend his record, urging voters to back him and saying he and US President Donald Trump had two years left to work together to topple Iran's rulers . PLAN DRAWS CRITICISM On Sunday, more than 100 economists, including former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu's proposal. They said it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel's economic standing in the world. "As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the living standards of Israeli citizens would plummet dramatically, and the state's ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged," the letter read. "Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organizations, that will not help in the slightest." Netanyahu's main rival in Tuesday's election, [USN:L6N46303T TEXT:"Gadi Eisenkot"], called the crypto plan "madness" and said he feared that the "BibiCoin policy" would drive companies abroad and undermine national security. Opposition leader Yair Lapid said: "Netanyahu has gone off the rails ... He promises the citizens of Israel before these elections that they'll be standing in line for an hour and a half for bread, like in Russia and Iran." Opinion polls point to a potential stalemate in the election with neither Netanyahu's ruling coalition nor an opposition alliance securing a governing majority in parliament.

item.title: British pin hopes of late SailGP lift on training blitz
item.description: Britain have struggled off the start line this season but the defending champions were the first to grab a week of intensive training at SailGP's new performance facility as they pursue a Grand Final berth, skipper Dylan Fletcher said.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Smith
item.content:encoded: Britain have struggled off the start line this season but the defending champions were the first to grab a week of intensive training at SailGP's new performance facility as they pursue a Grand Final berth, skipper Dylan Fletcher said. With only two events left, in Dubai and Abu Dhabi next month, the British are fifth in the championship, just behind the US and Sweden, in pursuit of a top-three finish that would earn a place in the winner-takes-all Grand Final. "We put our name down early to get one of these slots and I think that it's a really good opportunity," Fletcher told Reuters at the start of a week practising in Pensacola, Florida. SailGP gives crews very little practice on board their F50 catamarans, which can hit more than 100 kph when they lift above the water on foils, a gap the new facility aims to bridge. "We haven't had the season that we've been happy with at the moment. And this in reality feels like a great opportunity, not just on the water, but off the water," said Fletcher, ahead of the team's first 2-1/2-hour F50 session. "We're mainly focused on light wind starting... We've seen that as much as we've been still quite good at overtaking, the reality is it's all about the start," said Fletcher. "The Aussies have been the standout performers and you know that shows," he added of how the season's leaders start. The British are seeking short-term gains with their week in Pensacola, which can offer the lighter wind conditions that are the norm in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, as well as looking ahead to next season, which starts in Hong Kong in January. "We want to try and finish this season strong regardless of how it goes... to start off on the right foot (next season) because we obviously haven't been sailing at the level that we expect," Fletcher said. Despite the team's dip in form, Fletcher has not given up. "If we sail well enough to win the Grand Final, then we will be in the Grand Final. The momentum is almost more important going into those last two events," the 38-year-old said. "If you look at how the results generally go, I'd say if we made the final in both (Dubai and Abu Dhabi), it would be surprising if we weren't in the Grand Final," he added. While Spain's Los Gallos have "pretty much qualified", they have "everything to lose", Fletcher said, adding that the "British underdogs" had "absolutely nothing to lose". The British are focusing particularly on the pre-start "trigger" manoeuvre used to make sure the boat hits the line at top speed, along with Fletcher's positioning on the course. "We're going to try and execute that and have a bit of a change in our strategy," Fletcher said, adding: "Hopefully we can just tip the scales back in our favour, and we'll be away and looking like the team that we know we can be."

item.title: Rybakina brushes aside Fernandez to retain Ningbo crown
item.description: The title is her first as world number one ahead of the WTA Finals next month.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Elena Rybakina blazed past unseeded Canadian Leylah Fernandez 6-2 6-2 in the Ningbo Open final on Sunday to retain her title and lift her first trophy as the world number one ahead of the WTA Finals next month. The victory in Ningbo also helped the Kazakh to take a big step towards securing the year-end number one ranking, further burnishing a spectacular season in which she won the Australian Open title before adding the US Open crown to reach the summit. "It's amazing to play in front of you... it's my second year here and my second win," Rybakina told the crowd in the eastern Chinese city after collecting a tour-leading fourth title of the season and 15th overall. "It's such a special place for me. Thanks so much Ningbo." Rybakina's latest triumph is a timely lift after setbacks in Beijing and Wuhan, as she turns her attention to the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo this week before she launches her title defence at the season finale in Indian Wells, California, from November 8. TRADEMARK POWER Top seed Rybakina made the breakthrough with her trademark power in the fifth game and then unleashed a searing crosscourt backhand winner to go 4-2 up, before the 27-year-old wrapped up the opening set in 38 minutes. World number 30 Fernandez made a bright start to the next set but Rybakina absorbed the pressure and raised her level to force an error and break for 2-1, with the three-times Grand Slam champion breezing to victory from there. Fernandez, who won the Singapore Open last month, remained upbeat despite a disappointing showing in the final and backed herself to finish the season strongly after a gruelling run of matches in Ningbo. "I'd like to congratulate Elena for a wonderful week and a wonderful year. Congratulations to you and your team," the 24-year-old said, before addressing her own team. "We're having a good end of year. We've just got to keep going and keep working hard."

item.title: Serbia election: Main players, voter concerns and what is at stake
item.description: Serbia is holding parliamentary elections on Sunday, in which a popular student movement is seeking to end the rule of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic.
item.dc:creator: Canan Sevgili, Arda Dipova, Ivana Sekularac
item.content:encoded: Serbia is holding [USN:L6N46B017 TEXT:"parliamentary elections"] on Sunday, in which a popular student movement is seeking to end the rule of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic. Here are the main players, issues and stakes in the vote. WHO ARE THE MAJOR PLAYERS AND WHAT DO THEY STAND FOR? Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia: The Serbian Progressive Party (SNS)-led electoral list is campaigning on economic growth, higher wages and pensions, infrastructure investment and political stability. SNS leader Milos Vucevic has pledged 4% economic growth in 2027. Vucic, who resigned as president on September 27, is running to become prime minister. Students Win: Emerging from protests over the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse that killed 16 people, the anti-corruption movement has campaigned for accountability and transparent public procurement. The Democratic Party and Kreni Promeni movement have backed it rather than fielding their own lists. Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) – Ivica Dacic – Factor of Stability: A longstanding ally of the SNS, the pro-Russian SPS leads a coalition with Unified Serbia, the Social Democratic Party of Serbia and the Greens of Serbia. It campaigns on social justice, workers' rights and welfare, political stability, and national interests. European Serbia: A pro-European opposition alliance led by Marinika Tepic and Zdravko Ponos, bringing together the Party of Freedom and Justice, Serbia Centre, and the Solidarity, Self-Defence and Liberation movement. It advocates closer European integration, sanctions against Russia and democratic reforms. WHAT ARE PARTY LISTS AND HOW DO THEY WORK? Political parties, party coalitions, movements and other groups can submit party lists, or electoral lists comprising no more than 250 candidates. The election commission has approved a total of 18 lists. On election day, voters vote for one electoral list on the ballot, rather than individual candidates. WHAT ARE THE MAIN ISSUES FOR VOTERS? Corruption and government accountability have dominated the campaign since the Novi Sad disaster. Protesters accuse Vucic and his allies of corruption, controlling the media and mistreating demonstrators, allegations the authorities deny. Living standards, economic development and the fairness of the electoral process are also campaign issues. HOW WILL A VICTORY OR LOSS FOR VUCIC IMPACT SERBIA AT HOME AND ABROAD? A victory allowing Vucic to become prime minister would extend his political leadership and could preserve Serbia's balancing act between its ambition to join the European Union and maintain Belgrade's close ties with Russia and China. A defeat could pave the way for sweeping domestic reforms, including stronger institutions and measures against corruption.

item.title: Flávio e Lula disputam Presidência em eleição que pode ser definida pela abstenção
item.description: Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) decidem neste domingo quem governará o Brasil a partir de 5 de janeiro de 2027 após uma das campanhas eleitorais mais tensas e recheadas de acusações da história da política brasileira, sem que as pesquisas apontem um favorito claro e com um provável papel decisivo do comparecimento dos eleitores às urnas.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Simões
item.content:encoded: Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) decidem neste domingo quem governará o Brasil a partir de 5 de janeiro de 2027 após uma das campanhas eleitorais mais tensas e recheadas de acusações da história da política brasileira, sem que as pesquisas apontem um favorito claro e com um provável papel decisivo do comparecimento dos eleitores às urnas. Senador de oposição e filho mais velho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio, de 45 anos, largou na frente após um resultado surpreendente no primeiro turno, disputado há três semanas, quando terminou na liderança com 47,03% dos votos, contra 45,16% de Lula. O atual presidente e candidato à reeleição, que completará 81 anos na próxima terça e que busca um quarto mandato presidencial, reduziu gradativamente a distância para o rival nas pesquisas de intenção de voto mais recentes, o que leva a corrida a um cenário incerto. “O que o povo fez comigo nesses dias é uma coisa que não tem como pagar, é muita generosidade, é muito carinho, é muito amor e eu serei eternamente grato ao comportamento do povo”, disse o petista a jornalistas após votar na manhã deste domingo, em São Bernardo do Campo (SP), berço político do Partido dos Trabalhadores. As [USN:L2N46A047 TEXT:"pesquisas divulgadas na véspera"] da votação deste domingo mostraram um empate técnico com vantagem numérica de Flávio sobre Lula de no máximo dois pontos percentuais nos votos válidos, com 51% a 49%. "Flávio é ligeiramente favorito, ele não é francamente favorito", disse o cientista político Carlos Melo, do Insper. "Quando você olha para as pesquisas, mais do que o número você tem que olhar para a tendência. A tendência é o Flávio caindo, ou praticamente paralisado, e o Lula subindo muito devagar", acrescentou, apontando que não é possível prever se essa tendência resultará em uma virada a favor de Lula neste domingo. Um dos fatores cruciais a ser observado, na avaliação de Melo, será o comparecimento às urnas, já que historicamente o eleitorado que tende a apoiar mais Lula e o PT costuma ter um comparecimento menor. Não à toa, a campanha de Lula vem concentrando esforços em incentivar pessoas que não votaram no primeiro turno a comparecerem na seção eleitoral neste domingo. No primeiro turno, mais de 33,4 milhões de eleitores não foram votar, uma abstenção de 21,08%, em um total de mais de 158,7 milhões de eleitores aptos a votar. Neste domingo, no entanto, foi Flávio Bolsonaro quem fez um apelo para que os eleitores compareçam às urnas. "Faça chuva ou faça sol, bora sair de casa para votar, que o Brasil vai mudar e o Brasil vai vencer", disse o senador, após votar no Rio de Janeiro, repetindo apelo já feito em suas redes sociais na véspera, em meio à previsão de chuvas fortes nas regiões Sul e Sudeste, onde teve desempenho melhor que Lula. "Chegou a hora da mudança de verdade", afirmou o candidato, ao lado da esposa Fernanda e da mãe, Rogéria. As três semanas de campanha do segundo turno foram bastante diferentes dos meses que antecederam o primeiro turno, realizado no dia 4 de outubro. No caso de Lula, uma guinada em direção a uma mobilização maciça nas redes sociais e em eventos de rua, que ocorreu sem participação direta do núcleo duro da campanha no primeiro turno, contrastou com uma primeira fase de campanha que o próprio Lula reconheceu em reunião do PT como a "menos organizada" de que participou desde 1989. Na véspera da eleição, antes de participar de evento de campanha em Copacabana, Lula afirmou que "o povo assumiu para si a responsabilidade de fazer a campanha". Um dos destaques da campanha petista no segundo turno foi o impulso nas redes, liderada pelo canal de WhatsApp "Exército do Lula", criado pelo deputado federal reeleito André Janones (Rede-MG), que juntou mais de 10 milhões de pessoas para ouvir as "missões" que Janones dá para os apoiadores cumprirem nas redes. A campanha de Flávio chegou a entrar no TSE pedindo a suspensão do canal. A guinada digital da campanha petista teve como ápice Lula -- crítico público do uso frequente de celular que se orgulhava de não ter o aparelho -- ganhando um de presente do governador reeleito do Piauí, Rafael Fonteles (PT), e passando a fazer vários vídeos no formato selfie para apoiadores. Do lado de Flávio, após a inesperada liderança no dia 4, o senador deu declarações que geraram polêmica, como quando disse que, se eleito, usará a força que terá no próximo Congresso para alterar a Constituição. Posteriormente, afirmou que iria propor mudanças constitucionais como o fim da reeleição e a redução da maioridade penal. Também acabou mudando de posição em temas pautados por Lula, como o fim da escala de trabalho 6x1, para o qual ele votou a favor no Senado, apesar de, num passado muito recente, ter se declarado contrário. O senador, por outro lado, também conseguiu mobilizar grandes públicos em atos de campanha em todo o país, no que foi uma marca da campanha de ambos os lados. JUDICIALIZAÇÃO Em uma campanha marcada por grande movimentação das duas campanhas contra os adversários no TSE, que levou o presidente da corte Kassio Nunes Marques a pedir que as campanhas moderassem a quantidade de ações, há receios de que, independentemente do vencedor, ocorram novos embates mesmo após a declaração do resultado. A expectativa de uma margem apertada a favor do eleito também leva a crer que isso possa ocorrer. "A expectativa é de que vai ser uma eleição tensa", disse Creomar de Souza, analista político da Dharma Political Risk. "Acho que a gente ainda vai ter algum nível de discussão política, algum nível de embate jurídico", avaliou. Tanto Flávio quanto Lula não hesitaram em se acusar mutuamente de ladrão, corrupto e mentiroso ao longo de uma campanha em que propostas e discussões sobre o país ficaram em segundo plano. Denúncias de irregularidades contra os candidatos e seus familiares foram amplamente explorados, levando, nos últimos dias, a uma guerra de narrativas sobre a abertura de sigilos das duas partes. Em uma eleição que mais uma vez marcou a importância das redes sociais no processo político, a Meta (META.O) , proprietária do Facebook, do Instagram e do WhatsApp também ficou no foco, após a campanha de Lula apontar que teve sua atuação restrita nas plataformas da empresa, levando a big tech norte-americana a prestar esclarecimentos ao TSE. ELEITORES FALAM EM DEMOCRACIA E MUDANÇA Eleitores relatavam uma votação tranquila neste domingo, sem as filas vistas no primeiro turno, quando foi preciso votar também para deputado federal e estadual, senadores e governador. Neste segundo turno, apenas cinco Estados e o Distrito Federal têm votação para governador, além da eleição para presidente. A bibliotecária aposentada Hilda Corrêa, de 80 anos, fez questão de votar em Brasília, mesmo com o voto não sendo obrigatório a partir dos 70 anos. "Eu exerço essa cidadania minha desde que eu comecei a votar. E eu passei um tempo em que a gente não votava, quando eu era mais jovem, por causa da ditadura...Agora, tem que votar todo tempo. Pela democracia", disse ela, que anunciou voto em Lula. "Ele vai ser muito melhor do que essa turma da bala que está aí." Já o também aposentado José Carlos Jarra, de 61 anos, votou em Flávio Bolsonaro em São Paulo. "A gente precisa da mudança. Eu gostaria que ele (Flávio) mudasse a segurança, olhasse mais pelos aposentados, pelo salário mínimo, que aqui no Brasil é uma vergonha. Também rezo para que o Flávio e o Senado mexam neste Supremo Tribunal Federal", afirmou ele.

item.title: Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from Congo
item.description: Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on Sunday as Uganda tightened Ebola precautions.
item.dc:creator: Elias Biryabarema
item.content:encoded: Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on Sunday as Uganda tightened Ebola precautions. Uganda says it is Ebola-free after [USN:S8N41P031 TEXT:"declaring an end"] to its latest outbreak in July but there has been concern among health experts after two people who had recently passed through the country later tested positive in [USN:SPN45F00J TEXT:"Kenya"] and [USN:L8N4682IW TEXT:"Nigeria"]. Uganda says it investigating the Nigerian case which involves the wife of a Swiss diplomat who visited the country last month. Ugandan officials said they were reviewing genomic sequencing, travel information, interactions and movements in coordination with Nigerian authorities and international partners. Swiss authorities had said the woman contracted the virus in Uganda. Baryomunsi pushed back, saying Switzerland was "speaking prematurely". He said the woman's relatives from West Nile visited her in Kansanga, a suburb of Kampala, and that those relatives had visited Congo. "What evidence do they have that she never travelled there?" he said. "We should speak science, not politics." Kenya's first Ebola patient had travelled from Congo to Uganda and taken a flight from Entebbe airport to Nairobi on Oct. 3. The patient died two days later. Both the Kenyan and the Nigerian cases travelled through the same Ugandan airport on the same day but there was no physical interaction between the two, Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, told the press conference, citing a review of the airport's CCTV system. Baryomunsi said all 60 contacts linked to a [USN:L6N469174 TEXT:"Kenyan Ebola case"] had completed their 21-day monitoring period and been discharged. "The ministry has intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings. All travellers intending to enter Uganda by air, land or water must complete the passenger locator form," he said. [USN:L1N46915U TEXT:"Genomic analysis"] of Nigeria's only confirmed Ebola case showed the virus was closely related to the strain detected in Kenya's index case, though Nigerian authorities said there was no evidence that the Kenya case travelled to Nigeria or had a direct connection. Uganda borders Congo, where the outbreak began, and has previously battled Ebola outbreaks.

item.title: Newlands to provide test of more than bat and ball for Australia
item.description: The third test will be held at the scene of the Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal.
item.dc:creator: Nick Said
item.content:encoded: Australia return to the scene of one of the darkest days in the country’s cricket history when the series-deciding third test against South Africa starts at Newlands on Tuesday. The battle may be mental as much as one of skill for several of the Australian players, not least former captain Steve Smith, who was at the centre of the Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal in 2018. Current skipper Pat Cummins was part of that side, as were fellow seamer Josh Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon, though they say they had no knowledge of the attempt to alter the condition of the ball with a piece of sandpaper. Smith bore the brunt of the considerable fallout in Australia eight years ago and having not reached the heights he might have expected on this tour, averaging a little over 20 with the bat, he would see this as the perfect time to put that right. There has so far been little chatter in South Africa about Sandpapergate but that could change at Newlands, where the first three days’ ticket sales have been strong after sparse crowds at the first two tests in Durban and Gqeberha. "He'll be fine," Australia opener Travis Head said of Smith. "I think he showed that in 2019 in England. We support him. He's been through a lot in that space and handles it well. Sometimes it brings the best out of him, as we've seen in the past." The series is level at 1-1 after big wins for both sides in the opening two games and Australia wicketkeeper Alex Carey told reporters on Sunday that it looked to be another good test-match pitch. "We are still a couple of days out but it looks another great surface," he said. "If you look back at Durban it was a five-day test match and a great contest between bat and ball. The same in Port Elizabeth (Gqeberha) and this should be no different." There has never been a test match played at Newlands in October, and just three in November, all against Australia. The tourists won the first two in 1902 and 1921, but the most recent November fixture was an eight-wicket victory for South Africa in 2011 when Australia were famously bowled out for 47 in their second innings. South Africa will be without fast bowler Anrich Nortje, who injured his groin in the second test. Captain Temba Bavuma said they would pick horses for courses in terms of his replacement. "You’ve got guys like Gerald (Coetzee), Pato (Dane Paterson), as well as (Corbin) Bosch, and we have Sen (Senuran Muthusamy) as well, so the options are there," he said. "Whoever we decide, we’ll be confident they form part of our best XI for the conditions."

item.title: Beirut's $13 chicken sandwich becomes symbol of Lebanon divide
item.description: Seven years after Lebanon’s devastating financial meltdown, a debate over a chicken sandwich has exposed an increasingly stark divide between those who can still spend freely and those struggling to get by.
item.dc:creator: Nazih Osseiran, Raghed Waked, Emilie Madi
item.content:encoded: Seven years after Lebanon’s [USN:L6N41Y0N8 TEXT:"devastating financial meltdown"], a debate over a chicken sandwich has exposed an increasingly stark divide between those who can still spend freely and those struggling to get by. A trendy health restaurant wanted to offer its calorie-conscious customers a healthier take on the beloved Levantine wrap known as the shish taouk. So, The Glow Paradise launched the “Chic Taouk”, pricing it at around $13 — nearly double what an un-chic chicken sandwich typically goes for in Beirut. The pricy pun proved hard to swallow, with outraged critics accusing the restaurant of overcharging in a country where many households struggle to afford basic necessities. Yet while the debate raged on social media, customers kept buying. The Glow Paradise sold more than 20,000 Chic Taouk sandwiches in just 11 days, according to managing partner Hrag Jeghalian, who described the online exchanges as "natural marketing". The contrasting reactions touched a nerve in Lebanon, where years of financial turmoil, political dysfunction and conflict have reshaped the country's social landscape, hollowing out much of the middle class while leaving a smaller group of consumers able to sustain an affluent lifestyle. DEBATE PULLS FOCUS AWAY FROM URGENT CRISES Sami Nader, an economist at the Saint Joseph University of Beirut, said the throngs at The Glow Paradise belied another reality. “So you see people in the restaurant, but what you don't see is that 22 restaurants closed last month,” Nader told Reuters. Lebanon’s Instagram-active community was split between those accusing the restaurant of theft and others saying the sandwich was intended for those who could afford it. Some questioned whether the dispute itself reflected misplaced priorities in a country grappling with urgent crises, from Israel’s[USN:L6N45P03S TEXT:" occupation"] of large swaths of the country’s south to the endemic electricity and water crises. Lebanon’s 2019 financial collapse was prompted by decades of corruption and profligate spending by the ruling elite, and several rounds of conflict since then have worsened the country’s economic outlook. GDP has declined by nearly 40% since 2019 and inflation is expected to rise to 17.5% due to rising global energy and shipping prices eating away at people’s purchasing power, according to the World Bank. The figure is more than quadruple the [USN:L1N43A0MP TEXT:"global headline inflation"] rate flagged by the International Monetary Fund in July. Four in five households in Lebanon struggle to afford basic necessities, the UN children’s agency said in September. 'PEOPLE CAN'T KEEP UP' The country’s middle class has “disappeared,” Nader said, dismantled by a series of crises including the collapse of the financial system in 2019, the 2020 Beirut Port explosion and two wars in under two years. Monthly bills from private generator operators, which provide electricity to many homes and businesses during outages on Lebanon's failing national grid, jumped by nearly 20% in August 2026 alone, bringing rates nearly 60% higher than they were in February of this year, according to the kilowatt-hour prices set by Lebanon’s energy ministry. For many, that means paying for 24/7 electricity now costs several hundred dollars a month, in a country where the minimum wage is set at $400. “Everything has become expensive, and people can’t keep up,” said Fouad Fakhreddine, a 53-year-old restaurant worker from nearby Hamra. “We are now getting paid, then getting in debt over that just to get by.” The years of economic instability, he said, have produced “a class that is living, and a class that is not dead and waiting to die from the unbearable situation it is in.” (This story has been refiled to change the name in the byline to Emilie Madi from Ahmad Al Kerdi.)

item.title: Trump campaigns in Michigan a day after Obama rallies Democrats
item.description: US President Donald Trump will rally Republicans in eastern Michigan on Sunday, a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump will rally Republicans in eastern Michigan on Sunday, a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's midterm elections. Michigan has one of the nation's most competitive US Senate contests, an open-seat race between former US Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, and Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that will help decide control of the chamber. Despite repeatedly attacking El-Sayed from the Oval Office and at rallies across the country, the Republican president had not yet campaigned in Michigan this year. If he wins, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Trump has sought to paint El-Sayed as a Muslim extremist and repeatedly [USN:L1N4620ZA TEXT:"mocked his middle name,"] Mohamed, a common Muslim name. EL-SAYED SAYS AFFILIATION IS WITH THE US El-Sayed has dismissed the accusation and, in a recent advertisement, defended his religion, saying, "Faith is a thing there’s just too little of in Washington." Rogers has alleged without evidence that El-Sayed has [USN:L6N4661FE TEXT:"ties to the Muslim Brotherhood"], one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups. In an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, Rogers said El-Sayed had not sufficiently responded to questions about those allegations. "He's a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America," he said. El-Sayed has denied affiliation with the group, saying it is "shameful" for Rogers to question his allegiance to the United States. At Saturday's rally in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks on El-Sayed as an attempt by opponents to make him look "less patriotic and less American than they are." The former president compared it to his experience as the target of [USN:KBN23O2P2 TEXT:"false claims"] that he was born in Kenya. "We have seen this movie before," Obama said. "I starred in it ... This stuff didn't work on me. Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul." MANUFACTURING INVESTMENTS Trump's rally in Port Huron, part of an area of Michigan that he won in the 2024 presidential election with more than 66% of the vote, will also highlight the US-Canada tariff standoff. The trade fight has affected the Detroit-based [USN:L6N44N11O TEXT:"US auto industry,"] prompting Rogers to distance himself from the president's policy. Rogers on Sunday hailed Trump's tariffs for securing manufacturing investments for Michigan by Chevrolet and Detroit Diesel, but said "the automobile portion of these Canadian tariffs worries me a little bit." "There's some good and there's some things we have to work on," he told "Meet the Press." In a Fox News interview ahead of Sunday's rally, Trump praised Rogers as someone who shares Michigan voters' beliefs. "He's going to be an amazing senator," Trump told the "Sunday Briefing" program. "Solid as a rock. Apple pie." Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US Senate and House of Representatives to overturn Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

item.title: How Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy sites deepened the rift with Trump
item.description: The two have long had a testy relationship, but Trump's frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure triggered a crisis that Kyiv's supporters fear could threaten vital US support.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: Relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy took a sharp downward turn in recent weeks, with each leader openly criticizing the other. The two have long had a testy relationship, but Trump's frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure triggered a crisis that Kyiv's supporters fear could threaten vital US support going forward. Here's how the relationship soured: WHAT IS THE HISTORY OF TRUMP-ZELENSKIY TENSIONS? Trump has been skeptical of US involvement in Ukraine ever since his first term when, shortly after taking office in early 2017, he was asked to provide lethal aid to Ukraine and approved the sale of Javelin missiles to Kyiv. “Everyone around him wanted him to do it, and they pushed him hard and he eventually signed off on selling them Javelins, very reluctantly,” said a former senior Trump administration official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. “He didn’t consider it a core US interest. It was a European issue.” Trump's first major encounter with Zelenskiy came in a July 2019 phone call in which the Republican president asked the Ukrainian leader to investigate his Democratic rival Joe Biden and his son Hunter, in exchange for military support Congress had authorized. That episode led to Trump's first impeachment. Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election. Trump also has fostered a relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin that runs against the norms of US foreign policy but echoes his warm ties with authoritarian leaders Xi Jinping of China and North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un. “Trump has always wanted better relations with Russia,” the former official said. WHAT DEEPENED THE RIFT BETWEEN THE TWO LEADERS? Trump's current frustration centers on Kyiv's [USN:S8N41C0VK TEXT:"attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure"]. Diesel prices have hit record highs since the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, and global energy costs spiked. US lawmakers in Trump's Republican party face voter anger over inflation ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. On September 13, Trump began publicly calling on Ukraine to stop targeting diesel infrastructure. The following week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was also concerned that Ukraine had hit US-linked oil shipments. Ukraine has refused to halt the strikes, saying its long-range drone campaign is its only viable response to nearly five years of Russian bombardment. Moscow was forced in July to ban diesel exports as part of a raft of measures to address domestic fuel shortages. Angered by Zelenskiy’s defiance, Trump on October 9 announced a deal to buy diesel from Moscow, issuing a temporary general license that allows Russian diesel to reach the global market. He also waived sanctions on Russia authorized by a bill he signed into law in September. Suriya Jayanti, a former US official who runs a power sector company in Ukraine, said Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s power grid have increased, despite Trump unilaterally announcing an [USN:FWN45X008 TEXT:"energy ceasefire"] on October 11. "It is clear to everyone in Kyiv that the goal is not actually an energy ceasefire, but it is really just an effort to hobble Ukraine and give Russia a decisive advantage," said Jayanti, who is also a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank. HAS THE US THREATENED TO CUT OFF SUPPORT TO UKRAINE? Zelenskiy has said Ukrainian military officials had been threatened by US counterparts, who said continuing the energy strikes would lead the US to cut off intelligence sharing. A US official familiar with the situation disputed Kyiv's account. Speaking on condition of anonymity, the US official said there has been no increase in pressure on Ukraine. “We don't have to pressure Zelenskiy. If he wants to make a deal he'll make a deal. I think Putin is putting a ton of pressure on him and he (Zelenskiy) is putting some pressure on Russia but Russia doesn't seem to be minding it as much even though they are getting hit." On Thursday, Trump said he had asked SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to restore Ukraine’s access to the company's Starlink satellite system. Starlink's disruption temporarily hampered Kyiv's military drone operations and spurred fears that Kyiv would be left defenseless against Russia's attacks going into the winter. WHAT IS THE STATUS OF MOSCOW-KYIV PEACE TALKS? Peace efforts have continued but so far have not yielded tangible results. At talks in Oslo on October 20, Ukraine presented new proposals, and Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner repeated Trump's demand that Ukraine stop attacking Russian diesel refineries. The next day, envoy Witkoff – a close friend of Trump's - met Putin in St. Petersburg. Putin agreed to release detained American Stephen Hubbard in what the two countries called a goodwill gesture. Zelenskiy said on Friday that negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US would meet in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, a possible precursor to a meeting of the three countries’ leaders. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February.

item.title: Jordan church attack survivor says her cousin died before her eyes
item.description: When gunmen opened fire on a church in Jordan, Sahar al-Halsa hid behind a pillar as she heard the shooting and people screaming in panic during a funeral service for her cousin's daughter.
item.dc:creator: Abdelhadi Ramahi
item.content:encoded: When gunmen opened fire on a church in Jordan, Sahar al-Halsa hid behind a pillar as she heard the shooting and people screaming in panic during a funeral service for her cousin's daughter. When she rushed outside in the chaos, she said she spotted the assailants and another cousin lying on the ground wounded. "I went to him and said: 'Assem, Assem, my darling, answer me'," she said. She said he opened his eyes to look at her, but then "he was gone". Friday's attack on the Greek Orthodox place of worship in Karak governorate, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital Amman, prompted King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, to order security forces to respond with an "iron fist" to what authorities described as extremist terrorism. PRIEST SENDS MESSAGE OF LOVE AND PEACE Nine people died in the shooting that witnesses said lasted for several minutes. The funeral services were held on Sunday. Eight of the victims’ coffins were wrapped in Jordanian flags before they were buried in a graveyard in the village of Hamoud, where the attack took place. Mourners and priests gathered at the scene. Forty people were wounded in the rare attack on minority Christians. Speaking from her home, from where the red dome of St George's church is visible, al-Halsa concluded that God must have saved her. "My life starts now, because I was going to die," she said, speaking beside her husband Ziad al-Halsa. A statue of Jesus on a cross was displayed on a shelf. Authorities have said they are still searching for the attackers, adding it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. There has been no immediate claim of responsibility. Ziad said he ran the short distance to the church after he heard the gunfire, describing the overwhelming sense of relief when he realised Sahar, who he described as "the love of his life", was safe. "To my cousins, may God have mercy on them," he said. Such attacks are highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities there say they have foiled several Islamist plots in recent years. Speaking ahead of the funerals, priest Yuhanna Hamati said: "Our message from this church, from this place where this horrific crime was committed, is a message of love, peace, and reassurance. A message that we send to the whole world."

item.title: Employees group warns of major Swiss job losses if UBS relocates
item.description: As many as 12,000 UBS jobs in Switzerland could be at risk if tougher capital rules prompt the bank to relocate, according to the Swiss Bank Employees Association, or SBPV.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: As many as 12,000 UBS (UBSG.S) jobs in Switzerland could be at risk if tougher capital rules prompt the bank to relocate, according to the Swiss Bank Employees Association, or SBPV. In a letter to lawmakers first published at the weekend by newspaper NZZ am Sonntag, the association warned that a relocation, sale or merger of UBS could cost 10,000 to 12,000 of UBS's roughly 34,000 jobs in Switzerland. The letter, which was also seen by Reuters, described this as the "worst case" scenario, and comes on top of cuts already made at the bank as it completes it integration of fallen rival Credit Suisse, which it acquired in 2023. UBS, which has repeatedly said it wants to remain in Switzerland, declined to comment on the SBPV estimate. A UBS spokesperson said the bank would keep job cuts resulting from the Credit Suisse takeover as low as possible. UBS said it still expects around 3,000 layoffs in Switzerland under the integration and that these would occur over several years, largely via steps like natural turnover, early retirements and insourcing of jobs once held externally. The SBPV warning comes as a committee in the lower house of the Swiss parliament [USN:L1N45N0NB TEXT:"prepares"] to discuss how much capital UBS should have to hold to back its foreign subsidiaries. Last month, the upper house [USN:L8N45F0DE TEXT:"proposed"] UBS should back those units with 90% Common Equity Tier 1 capital. UBS suggested that is [USN:L1N45C05I TEXT:"too much"] and the bank's chairman has warned it would need to carefully [USN:L8N4590WE TEXT:"consider"] its future in Switzerland if the rules are too harsh. Some shareholders of the bank have called for UBS to [USN:L1N45N061 TEXT:"leave"] Switzerland, and the bank has been [USN:L1N46205Q TEXT:"drafting"] potential contingency plans including shifting its headquarters or merging with another lender, sources have told Reuters. The SBPV letter, which also said UBS had a duty to commit to its Swiss base, urged lawmakers to pursue a "viable compromise" that did not impose such a heavy burden on the bank.

item.title: Russia says it hit two cargo vessels and Ukrainian logistics hubs
item.description: The Russian Defence Ministry said on Sunday that its drones had struck a cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk in an overnight attack and another cargo vessel en route to the port of Odesa during the day.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Russian Defence Ministry said on Sunday that its drones had struck a cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk in an overnight attack and another cargo vessel en route to the port of Odesa during the day. The ministry said the vessels were being used to supply the Ukrainian army. Russian forces also hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight. The ministry said the facilities had been used for storage and distribution of dual-use cargo for the Ukrainian military. Reuters could not independently verify the Defence Ministry's information.

item.title: Four killed in two drone attacks in Russia's Belgorod region
item.description: A Ukrainian drone attack overnight on the Russian border city of Belgorod killed three people and injured 13, local authorities said on Sunday, while a separate drone strike later in the day killed another person and wounded one other in a nearby village.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A Ukrainian drone attack overnight on the Russian border city of Belgorod killed three people and injured 13, local authorities said on Sunday, while a separate drone strike later in the day killed another person and wounded one other in a nearby village. "Unfortunately, the death toll from last night's attack (in the city of Belgorod) has risen — another man who had been injured has died in hospital. This is a great tragedy for all the city's residents," Belgorod's mayor, Valentin Demidov, wrote on state-backed messaging app MAX. The overnight attack on Belgorod damaged 30 apartment buildings, 35 cars, four houses, three administrative buildings, eight commercial premises and three social facilities, regional governor Alexander Shuvayev said. In a separate incident on Sunday morning, one person was killed and another injured when a Ukrainian drone struck a car in the village of Voznesenovka near the town of Shebekino, local authorities said.

item.title: Most Gulf shares close lower as Saudi-Houthi fighting rages on
item.description: Most Gulf bourses ended lower on Sunday and Saudi Arabia's index registered its worst session in 18 months as fighting between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis showed no sign of abating.
item.dc:creator: Ateeq Shariff
item.content:encoded: Most Gulf bourses ended lower on Sunday and Saudi Arabia's index registered its worst session in 18 months as fighting between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis showed no sign of abating. Saudi air defences downed drones and missiles over Riyadh and the south on Sunday, [USN:L2N46A05D TEXT:"the Saudi-led coalition said"]. A day earlier, the Houthis said they [USN:L2N46A00K TEXT:"hit Saudi oil facilities and airports"] and the Saudi-led coalition said it downed two missiles. Saudi Arabia's benchmark index (.TASI) pared losses to finish 2.7% lower after falling as much as 3.4%. The index posted its worst intraday performance since April 2025, with heavyweight Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) falling 0.9%. GCC stocks stayed under pressure as tensions and shipping disruptions in key waterways kept investors wary. Fears of renewed US military action dented de-escalation hopes, with traders awaiting diplomatic progress, said George Pavel, general manager at Naga.com Middle East. In Qatar, the index (.QSI) reversed early losses to inch 0.1% higher. Outside the Gulf, Egypt's blue-chip index (.EGX30) plunged 3.6%, its biggest single-day fall since June 2025, with most of its constituents in negative territory. Saudi Arabia (.TASI) declined 2.7% to 9,439 Qatar (.QSI) inched 0.1% higher to 8,615 Egypt (.EGX30) dropped 3.6% to 49,234 Bahrain (.BAX) eased 0.2% to 1,849 Oman (.MSX30) retreated 1.4% to 7,278 Kuwait (.BKP) added 0.5% to 8,768

item.title: Brazil votes in tight runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro
item.description: Corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling dominated the race.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Griffin, Luciana Novaes Magalhaes, Marta Nogueira
item.content:encoded: Brazilians voted on Sunday in a tight runoff vote that could move Latin America's largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region. The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored [USN:L6N45Q04L TEXT:"a major upset at the start of the month"] by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round. A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security. WASHINGTON DENIES ACCUSATIONS OF MEDDLING Reuters on Saturday [USN:L1N4650X8 TEXT:"revealed a campaign"] within Trump's State Department to help get the Bolsonaros back in power. Trump has so far declined to endorse a candidate. Asked on Sunday who he hoped would win, Trump declined to say. "I don’t want to get into that, but we are watching," he told reporters in Washington. Brazil's election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from [USN:L1N43T0Q4 TEXT:"Jair Bolsonaro's 2025"] conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if elected. Trump has called the case a "witch hunt" and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. While this was later watered down, Trump unleashed [USN:L1N43P1HE TEXT:"new levies against Brazil this year"], citing unfair trade practices. Lula has cast the Trump administration’s proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labeling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying. “We can’t just hand Brazil over,” said Elenildes dos Reis, a 60-year-old lawyer in Sao Paulo who voted for Lula and said his victory would be a way of standing up to Trump and what she described as a rising wave of fascism. “It won’t just be our victory, it will be the world’s,” she said. On economic issues, despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters’ minds. Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns and has promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses. “We need change,” said Jose Carlos Jarra, a 61-year-old retiree in Sao Paulo who worked in healthcare and voted for Bolsonaro. He hoped the senator would tackle public security and do more for retirees, calling Brazil’s minimum wage “a disgrace.” In Rio de Janeiro, 75-year-old retiree Alba Marques said her vote for Bolsonaro was a vote against Lula's Workers' Party, not for Bolsonaro. "I can’t stand 40 years of a guy saying he’s going to fix Brazil anymore. The same promise," she said. CANDIDATES ARE NECK AND NECK Casting his ballot in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday, Bolsonaro urged people to come out to vote "come rain or shine." Lula voted in Sao Bernardo do Campo, near Sao Paulo, and thanked his supporters. "What the people did for me these past few days is something I can never repay," he told reporters. Polls show the candidates practically tied going into the runoff. Historical precedent favors Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote. Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%. The senator's first-round win [USN:L6N45Q08A TEXT:"sent Brazil's markets and currency soaring"] on expectations of pro-business reforms. His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him, or complicate governance for Lula.

item.title: Disenchanted Netanyahu supporters are prize of Israel election campaign
item.description: Labor has dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightwards, and there are now around half a dozen other parties courting Likud voters, from the center to the far right.
item.dc:creator: Emily Rose, Maayan Lubell
item.content:encoded: In the remote Negev Desert town of Dimona, long a bastion of Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party, disenchanted voters are going door-to-door campaigning for his top rival, hoping to bring down the veteran prime minister in Israel's election on Tuesday. The ballot is Israel's first since Hamas' October 7, 2023, surprise attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the militant group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran. The October 7 security breach saw Likud's popularity plummet. Opinion polls for months have predicted Netanyahu's coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties losing its majority. But his top rival, centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears. Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground. "We must have change. Bibi has to go," said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most his life. "Bibi has brought disaster to Israel." LIKUD LOYALISTS Assayag is part of a cohort of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot's party Yashar, which is neck-and-neck with Likud in the polls. It's a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the previous 2022 election cast a ballot for Likud. "I will never betray Likud," said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and the blame he receives from detractors for October 7 was unfair. Right-wing Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced centre-left Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations. Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightwards, and there are now around half a dozen other parties courting Likud voters, from the centre to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong. "Most people here vote for Likud just because that's how they were raised," said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. "The change will come when people start to think about their children's future rather than their parents' past." BATTLE FOR WAVERING LIKUDNIKS While Netanyahu has a hard core of supporters that can't be won over, the prize is undecided voters who "understand that we are in a state of crisis" and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot's Dimona campaign. Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute. Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided. It is in places just like Dimona where Eisenkot stands a chance to bite a chunk out of Likud's base, said Amotz Asa-El, a political scientist at the Hartman Institute. A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins from the Mizrahi community that "appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud's traditional electorate", said Asa-El. In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters. At a town hall during a visit to Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a leader of Mizrahi descent. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son. But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds. "Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love," he said. Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears. But even some who are sympathetic to Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel's youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms. "It's time for him to go," said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. "He's done a lot for Israel but it can't go on. I won't give my vote to someone almost 80-years-old."

item.title: Borr Drilling rig sinks off Gabon, one person dead and four missing
item.description: Borr Drilling's Prospector 5 rig sank late on Saturday off the coast of Mayumba, Gabon, killing one employee and leaving four others missing among the 115 people on board, three sources familiar with the matter said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Gnaneshwar Rajan, Colleen Goko
item.content:encoded: Borr Drilling's (BORR.N) Prospector 5 rig sank late on Saturday off the coast of Mayumba, Gabon, killing one employee and leaving four others missing among the 115 people on board, three sources familiar with the matter said on Sunday. An Indian national, one of the five initially unaccounted for, has been found dead. The remaining four missing include three Gabonese nationals and one other expatriate, the sources said. The government has not confirmed the death, instead saying that five people remain missing and that search efforts were ongoing. "Preliminary information indicates that the rig experienced a punch-through event during preload activities, resulting in loss of stability and the subsequent sinking of the rig," the offshore drilling contractor said. The Prospector 5 oil and gas rig, owned and operated by Borr, is contracted to support BW Energy's (BWE.OL) drilling operations off Gabon. The rig had not yet begun drilling. Prospector 5 is located at the Dussafu Marin permit, a licence off the Gabon coast. BW Energy holds a 73.5% working interest in the licence, with Panoro Energy holding 17.5%. Gabon's Ministry of Petroleum and Gas said it had activated a crisis unit and ordered the navy to reinforce search and rescue operations at sea. The ministry also ordered a technical investigation, Petroleum and Gas Minister Clotaire Kondja said in a statement. The crisis unit brings together the ministry, the navy, state oil company Gabon Oil, BW Energy and Borr Drilling, Kondja said. The accident occurred at approximately 9:40 p.m. (2040 GMT) on Saturday in the Dussafu Marin permit area near the Mabomont production facility, the ministry said. "We are deeply concerned for those who remain unaccounted for and everyone affected by this incident," said Borr Drilling Chief Executive Bruno Morand. "Our immediate priority is supporting the ongoing search and rescue efforts and the welfare of all personnel involved." Panoro Energy (PENR.OL) said production had been halted, adding that there were no reports of damage or accidental discharges. No discharge of harmful substances has been observed, the ministry said, adding that pollution-response resources remained deployed to protect the coastline and nearby Mayumba National Park.

item.title: Portuguese police clear Lisbon housing protest camp, arresting 25
item.description: Portuguese police cleared a camp in central Lisbon held to protest against the country's deepening housing crisis, baton-charging demonstrators in the early hours of Sunday and making 25 arrests.
item.dc:creator: Sergio Goncalves, Miguel Pereira
item.content:encoded: Portuguese police cleared a camp in central Lisbon held to protest against the country's deepening housing crisis, baton-charging demonstrators in the early hours of Sunday and making 25 arrests. Portugal is grappling with one of Europe's most acute home affordability crises, as prices have more than doubled since 2017 while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, with young people among the hardest hit. The Portuguese protests echo recent demonstrations in [USN:L1N45U0F8 TEXT:"Spain"] over home shortages and surging rents. There have also been protests in cities including [USN:L2N46A01A TEXT:"Paris"], where small student demonstrations over school conditions broadened into wider protests against the government's economic policies.
