In Portugal, dozens of officers, some with police dogs, moved in on the camp in Rossio Square shortly after 2 a.m. (0200 GMT), having warned protesters their tents would be dismantled if they weren't removed and threatening disobedience charges for those who resisted. POLICE SAY OPERATIONS 'PROPORTIONATE' Protesters had pitched more than 100 tents after Saturday's protest march by thousands along one of Lisbon's main avenues. "We have an obligation to fight for what we believe in," said one marcher, Vitor Gomes, 21, a multimedia communications student, adding that housing speculation, wealth concentration and rising inequality made him pessimistic about the future. Police said the operation was "proportionate" and that 25 people arrested for disobedience were later released and are due in court on Monday. POLICE SAY OFFICERS AND PROTESTERS INJURED A smaller camp of about 50 tents was also dismantled in Porto's Praca D. Joao I, where police made six arrests. While police reported seven minor injuries among officers and protesters in the two operations, activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 people were hurt and called for a fresh protest outside parliament on Tuesday. "Choosing the early hours of the morning to unleash dogs and baton-charge peaceful protesters is a political decision. It shows this government would rather repress those denouncing the housing crisis than address it," the group said. Protesters say soaring rents and higher living costs are squeezing households and turning housing into a growing source of discontent, with young people among those hardest hit. The Bank of Portugal estimates a shortfall of 300,000 homes nationwide, equivalent to Lisbon's entire housing stock. The protesters are demanding that the government scrap a [USN:L6N45M1AX TEXT:"bill"] to make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first parliamentary reading, although the far-right Chega party abstained.

item.title: Obama unloads on Trump while stumping for Democrats ahead of midterms
item.description: Barack Obama framed the Nov. 3 midterm elections vote as a "circuit breaker" to "at least rein in some of the foolishness" of Trump's presidency.
item.dc:creator: Dan Catchpole
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump has been telling voters to view the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot, and on Saturday one of his Democratic predecessors did just that. Ten days out from the elections that will determine control of the closely divided Congress, Barack Obama took to the campaign trail to accuse the Republican president of corruption, deride his strategy for Iran and skewer the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations. Obama stumped for Democratic candidates at rallies in Cleveland and Detroit, lampooning the Trump administration. Campaigning in Michigan for US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Obama framed the November 3 vote as a "circuit breaker" to "at least rein in some of the foolishness" of Trump's presidency. "We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government," Obama said. Obama, president from 2009 until Trump began his first term in 2017, remains one of the most popular figures among Democrats. They hope that bringing him into the race can fire up their supporters for a tight US Senate race in which El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative. The former president obliged the Michigan crowd by playing to Democrats' frequently repeated criticisms of Trump and of Republicans' willingness to go along with him. "We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, on your dime, like this," Obama said. "Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this ... Now the party seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government." The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But in a Truth Social post on early Sunday morning, Trump called Obama a "grossly incompetent President" and labeled El-Sayed a "Muslim Brotherhood Jihadist, who hates Jews and Blacks and AMERICANS and TRUMP". A Reuters/Ipsos poll in August found that 63% of Americans think the president and his family have [USN:L6N44F13X TEXT:"inappropriately profited"] from cryptocurrency since he returned to the White House last year and that 69% believe his policy decisions are influenced by his private business dealings. Obama also ridiculed the administration's claims of victory against Iran. He argued that the war has given Iran more economic leverage because its threats to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have unsettled oil exporters. "Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world," Obama said. In his social media post, Trump derided the Obama administration's approach to the Iranians, saying that he "paid off Iran with $Billions, and gave them a road to a Nuclear Weapon" with his 2015 [USN:L6N42K0ZD TEXT:"Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action"] accord with Iran. The United States withdrew from the 2015 agreement during Trump's first term. The former president also accused the Trump administration of emphasizing unimportant matters, sarcastically calling Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth someone "laser-focused on important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops" and ridiculing White House renovations as tacky. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Obama said.

item.title: Serbia votes in historic election as students seek to end Vucic's long grip on power
item.description: Serbian voters turned out in force on Sunday as a mass student protest movement sought to unseat longtime populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade.
item.dc:creator: Ivana Sekularac, Edward Mcallister, Aleksandar Vasovic
item.content:encoded: Serbian voters turned out in force on Sunday as a mass student protest movement sought to unseat longtime populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade. The [USN:L8N46618N TEXT:"snap parliamentary elections"], called by Vucic in September, come after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. The students have since [USN:L8N4650K6 TEXT:"gained widespread support"]. Unusually long lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country. Pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put turnout at 27.3% by 11 a.m. (1000 GMT), nearly double the 15.1% at the same time in the previous election in 2023. Even Vucic waited in line for nearly two hours to vote. First indications of results are expected around two hours after polls close at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT). A student victory would be a profound political shift in the Balkan country of some 6 million people, reminiscent of the [USN:L1N40V01B TEXT:"defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban"] in April. It could also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have [USN:L6N464038 TEXT:"taken to the streets"] in recent weeks to protest, [USN:L2N46A01A TEXT:"in some cases violently"], against poor education standards and a lack of prospects. "It is very important for all people to come and vote if they want to change something and I think it is a time for change," said lawyer Marija Cvjeticanin at a Belgrade polling station. Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, is a strong incumbent. Many voters thank him for pulling Serbia from economic obscurity and orchestrating a period of sustained modernisation including new highways, railways, schools and hospitals. OPINION POLLS PREDICT TIGHT RACE Vucic has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare. Internationally, he has sought closer ties with China, a major investor, and remained close to Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas. At the same time, he still says he wants to join the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner, but the bloc has become [USN:L6N3Z90I6 TEXT:"increasingly frustrated"] with a lack of reform. "I voted for our children, our young people...our children deserve peace and work, only Vucic can bring that," said Hatidza, a Roma woman. The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling, but they have been quieter on their international ambitions. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although it is not clear who would be prime minister should they win. "I hope that today will pass in a democratic atmosphere, in peace, and that we will legitimately elect a new government in Serbia," Srdanovic said after casting his vote in Novi Sad, adding that the scenes suggested there would be a record voter turnout in the country's recent history. After casting his vote, Vucic said he would respect the result. "If we lose we will acknowledge the will of the electorate, if we win no one will take it (from us)," he said. Opinion polls ahead of the vote predicted a tight race. The head of the Election Commission, Vladimir Dimitrijevic, said voting had so far passed without incident, but monitoring bodies CeSID and CRTA pointed to incidents related to the electoral roll and secrecy of voting. STUDENT PROTESTS INCREASE PRESSURE ON VUCIC The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say [USN:L8N4612LD TEXT:"repression has worsened"] in the period since. "For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by the rules of democracy," said actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, at a Belgrade polling station. Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He says the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss. "This has been one of the most difficult but the most emotional campaigns," Vucic told his supporters on Thursday. "We stood against those who wanted to destroy Serbia."

item.title: Saudi says Riyadh airport partly reopens despite renewed Houthi threats
item.description: Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday even as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, saying it remained a "military target".
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday even as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, saying it remained a "military target". King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had halted operations on October 10 following an attack claimed by the Houthis that killed 13 people, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the militant group continued unabated. The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran , turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war. FLIGHT TRACKING DATA SHOWS LITTLE TRAFFIC After Saudi authorities announced the partial resumption of operations at the airport, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree vowed the facility would "never be safe" and urged airlines, airport staff and travellers not to use it. Late on Saturday, the airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday. Despite the announcement, flight tracking data from Flightradar24 showed little traffic at the airport on Sunday. The Saudi-led coalition said earlier this month that the Houthis had carried out 20 attacks on the airport between October 1 and 11. MISSILE AND DRONE ATTACKS CONTINUE Saudi civil defense said on Sunday that shrapnel from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis over Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah injured two people and damaged residential buildings and vehicles. Civil defense authorities earlier issued emergency alerts for Riyadh and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran on Sunday, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed. The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait. It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements. Saudi Arabia has stepped up its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz. The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government, after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa a year earlier.

item.title: Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
item.description: Two US State Department officials pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting Brazil's election in their favor.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Stargardter
item.content:encoded: Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter. Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration. The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who [USN:L1N3ZM12Y TEXT:"oversees Brazil policy"], and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported. Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said. In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said. After Bolsonaro received a [USN:S0N3UJ08N TEXT:"27-year sentence in September 2025"], the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said. Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department. State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections." Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests. Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration. Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed." SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of " free speech diplomacy ," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies. The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions. Moraes did not respond to a comment request. Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America. Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court. Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power. Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption. Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so. Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment. Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said. The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts. A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy." TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime. Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups. In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time. Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those [USN:S0N3ON011 TEXT:"announced against Mexican cartels"] in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said. Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees. The State Department announced the designation the following day. Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision. BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil. Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said. Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS (JBSS.O) - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down. Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March [USN:S0N3ZG01R TEXT:"Brazil barred Beattie"] from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison. Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity. Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory. "Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually."

item.title: Audi defends decision to stand by Trump on $4 billion US factory in Georgia
item.description: Trump's tariffs dealt Audi a $1.4 billion blow last year.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, David Shepardson, Rachel More
item.content:encoded: The head of German automaker Audi defended on Sunday the company's planned $4 billion investment in a new US plant, announced by President Donald Trump as he campaigns for the November midterm elections . Audi Chief Executive Gernot Doellner stood alongside Trump at a rally in Perry, near Macon in central Georgia on Saturday, as the US president said Audi, part of the Volkswagen Group , planned to build an assembly plant in Georgia that will produce 200,000 SUVs annually. "This decision was preceded by many months of careful planning and intense negotiations," Doellner told reporters on Sunday. "If the American president invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands." A final decision on the investment will have to be taken by Volkswagen's supervisory board for it to go ahead. Georgia has competitive election races for the US Senate and its governor and Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy and boosting US manufacture. In Germany, the tariffs have added to the pressures on European industry and [USN:L8N4690LO TEXT:"tension between"] Volkswagen management and workers, who face job cuts and possible plant closures. Trump's tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and parts cost Audi around €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion) last year as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico, Audi has said. Critics of the tariffs say they have also been damaging in the US where they have increased vehicle prices and delayed some automaker investments. A spokesperson for Germany's IG Metall union said the decision by Doellner to extend a hand to Trump during the election was "hard to understand". "Trump has never failed to make it clear what he is after: he wants to weaken our domestic economy, particularly the automotive sector," the spokesperson said. Christiane Benner, head of the IG Metall union and Volkswagen's deputy supervisory board chair, said it was "right and necessary" to improve the company's position on the US market with a new plant. "However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set out," she said. Doellner declined to give full details on the investment deal with the US, including whether it involves tariff relief for the company. AN OPPORTUNITY IF GERMAN WORKERS BENEFIT Olaf Lies, state premier of the German state of Lower Saxony, Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, said that expanded production in the US was an opportunity provided German workers also benefit. "Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here and must not displace them," he said. Audi said the investment will create approximately 4,500 jobs. Construction is scheduled to begin next year, with production starting in the early 2030s, Audi said. The plant is expected to assemble the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, a US official told Reuters. Audi also plans to build 25,000 vehicles a year in neighboring South Carolina, the official said. Some of the vehicles, now built in Europe, would be exported, the official added. Those vehicles will be assembled at a $2 billion plant of VW's off-road brand Scout Motors that is under construction in Blythewood, near the state capital, Columbia, the official said. "We regard the region as a key market for profitable growth," Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said. "A potential Audi plant in the US would create further conditions for this." A gold Audi with manufacturer licence plates was parked outside Trump's rally on Saturday.

item.title: Protests sweep Italian cities amid heavy security presence, some violence reported
item.description: Authorities deployed a heavy police presence and many shops closed as a precaution.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Protests against war and rising living costs took place in major Italian cities on Saturday, with some incidents of violence, a week after unrest erupted across the country. Authorities deployed a heavy police presence and many shops closed as a precaution against possible damage. The demonstrations, [USN:L8N4650S6 TEXT:"which followed clashes last weekend"] in which protesters fought with police, looted shops and vandalised property, were violent in Turin, Rome and Bologna, with clashes between officers and demonstrators. They were largely peaceful in Milan. Reuters witnesses did not observe any shops being looted or property vandalised. After calls for further demonstrations circulated on social media this week, authorities made extensive security arrangements and deployed large numbers of police officers to prevent a repeat of last weekend's violence. Earlier on Saturday, Italian police said they had detained a person allegedly linked to organising the "October 17 Movement" — last weekend's protests — and had taken them to police headquarters in Milan for questioning.

item.title: Around 1,200 Palestinians are displaced in Hebron as Israel begins military operation
item.description: The Palestinian Authority criticised the operation as a "collective punishment."
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Israeli military forced around 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian official said on Saturday, a day after a Palestinian attack [USN:L1N4690KO TEXT:"killed two Israeli"] soldiers. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday had said the military would launch a large-scale operation after the soldiers were killed when two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at a military checkpoint near the city. The Israeli military said the gunmen were shot dead. They also said the operation in the Al-Jaladah and Ein Deir Baha neighbourhoods near the military checkpoint at the entrance of Hebron was to search for militants and weapons. In a statement, it also said the military would carry out demolitions. The Palestinian Authority criticised the operation as a "collective punishment". Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, the head of Hebron's municipality, said around 1,300 faced losing their homes in addition to the 1,200 already displaced. He also said the Israeli operations were motivated by parliamentary elections on Tuesday when Netanyahu's right-wing coalition may lose his majority, opinion polls show. "Netanyahu and the radical ministers in his government are trying to win as many votes as possible from the settlers," Al-Jabari said. The non-governmental organisation the Palestinian Prisoners' Club said Israeli forces had arrested around 70 Palestinians on Friday and Saturday. Israeli officials have not commented on any arrests. NETANYAHU'S GOVERNMENT HAS PRESIDED OVER EXPANSION OF SETTLEMENTS Al-Jabari said the military had demolished shops, factories, homes, and roads in Hebron and that the response was disproportionate and unjustified. Residents in Hebron told Reuters that the military expelled many people with no connection to the Palestinian attackers. "We are calling on officials to stand by us because we are not involved in any of this. There are children. We are isolated; we don’t do anything. This is all arbitrary,” said Majdi Nasser, one of those driven from his home. Residents told Reuters they saw Israeli soldiers marking homes with a black X after their Palestinian occupants had been forced to leave. It was not immediately clear what the X mark meant. Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid [USN:L6N44Y077 TEXT:"expansion"] of settlements, deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this. Across the West Bank, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns, severely curtailing Palestinians' freedom of movement. Yousef Mur, a resident of the Palestinian town of Yatta, said the closures meant he was unable to reach Jerusalem with his daughter for her cancer treatment. "The situation is bad, and we are suffering. When we tried to cross, they fired stun grenades towards us, and my girl got scared on the way. They fired stun grenades towards people. The situation is very difficult," Mur said. (This story has been refiled to remove the repeated word 'when' in paragraph 2.)

item.title: Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
item.description: Trump boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and admires a Republican’s buttocks.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland, Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Jacob Bogage
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress. In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks. Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country: TRUMP'S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “[USN:L1N45M10K TEXT:"bad job"]” explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low [USN:S0N4310A5 TEXT:"poverty rate"], low [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"unemployment,"] record highs in the [USN:L6N45S0IV TEXT:"stock market"] and cheaper prices for some food items. But his sales pitch is colliding with voters' concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses. Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends. The disconnect was evident outside Trump's rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people. “Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family." RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE Trump's travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory. Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday. Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election. Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa. Notably absent from Trump's travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine. TRUMP'S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity. But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues. "I'm doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it's the same thing. It's massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There's something going on that's very special." The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens. At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty. Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday. Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them. FRANCE BECOMES A 'BETE NOIRE' FOR MIDTERMS Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods. But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade. “What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday. Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran. “They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world. TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic. This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton. At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.” “Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said. Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old." Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer's prowess beyond his golf game. Trump's focus over the years on people's physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents. Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton. "Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don't." That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies.

item.title: Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests across France
item.description: Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts and museums closing their doors.
item.dc:creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Yann Tessier, Crispian Balmer
item.content:encoded: Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Saturday, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of [USN:L1N46608H TEXT:"last week's unrest"]. The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high. The main demonstration took place on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality. The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon at a group of around 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed on a cold, rainy evening. In France's second city, Marseille, youths set fire to rubbish bins to block roads, and hurled rocks and bottles at security forces. Police said several stores, including two jewellery shops, were ransacked. Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse. "In almost every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence," said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment trouble. PARIS IN LOCKDOWN Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest on October 17. Nunez told reporters the violence was less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage. "What changed was anticipation," he said. He also said far-right activists had sought confrontations with leftist groups in the southern cities of Nice and Montpellier, opening a potential new front in the disturbances. Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers [USN:L2N46A00I TEXT:"boarding up storefronts"], [USN:L5N46A022 TEXT:"museums closing their doors"] and more than 20 metro stations shut. Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend. "There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris. Several of the capital's best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated. "Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans. PROTESTS RIPPLE ACROSS EUROPE The nationwide disorder began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris last month to denounce school conditions. It swiftly broadened into a wider protest against the government's economic policies and inspired demonstrations in neighbouring countries. On Saturday [USN:L6N46A05C TEXT:"Belgian police"] used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, with protests also taking place in a number of Italian cities for a second weekend, [USN:L2N46A02Y TEXT:"and in Albania"]. Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires next year, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world's richest nations. "Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters. FAR-RIGHT PARTY HOLDS CONGRESS Many demonstrators accused the government of overreacting to last week's turmoil, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants. "We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student. "My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added. The first authorised march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city. A [USN:L6N4690NC TEXT:"shooting"] west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl. "We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

item.title: Wall St Week Ahead Earnings flood, Fed meeting will test rickety AI market rally
item.description: US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a Federal Reserve meeting posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a Federal Reserve meeting posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally. Weakness in technology shares left investors [USN:L6N468196 TEXT:"on edge about the state of the AI trade"] that has driven the US equity bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary. The Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) posted a slim loss on Friday, a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest daily drop since June. Investors were disappointed by quarterly reports from Meta (META.O) and Lam Research (LRCX.O) . Meta is one of the hyperscalers spending massively to build out data centers, while Lam is a high-flying semiconductor company, one of a group that has been among the biggest AI stock winners. Three other hyperscalers -- Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) -- headline a packed week of quarterly results, including about one-third of S&P 500 companies. The Fed's interest rate policy meeting on Wednesday also could rattle markets. "There are a lot of balls in the air," said Nick Giorgi, chief equity strategist at Alpine Macro. "Next week, you have a lot more tech earnings, and right now the market is taking a discerning eye as it relates to all the spending that goes along with artificial intelligence," Giorgi said. "The market's just not giving the benefit of the doubt to companies that are spending a ton of money on building this all out, which to us is actually very healthy, but still does augur for some short-term pain." Investors also have their focus trained on the US midterm elections on November 3, with growing bets that the Democrats will wrest control of the US Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party. The series of market catalysts could ratchet up volatility over the next couple of weeks and challenge optimism that has helped lift the benchmark S&P 500 index (.SPX) up 11% in 2026. HYPERSCALERS ON THE HOT SEAT Robust US profit growth has underpinned the stock market's gains this year in the face of headwinds including spiking Treasury yields and rising energy costs stemming from the Middle East conflict. With more than 100 companies having posted results so far, third-quarter S&P 500 earnings are on pace to have climbed more than 32% from a year ago, according to LSEG IBES data. Next week is the busiest of the reporting season. "I think earnings will determine whether this ... tech pullback is a buying opportunity, or is there a deeper correction ahead," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management. "What we need is just another round of really strong earnings." Alphabet and Microsoft report on Wednesday. Amazon's results are due Thursday. Focus will be on the guidance the companies give on capital spending plans and whether they are seeing returns on the massive outlays. Capital spending from hyperscalers, expected to be around $800 billion this year, is boosting the bottom lines for a wide swath of companies involved in the AI buildout. But investors are wary of the sustainability of such spending amid mounting financing costs. "Earnings are critical to the overall confidence level of the AI trade and how much longer the spend will continue," said Kevin Mahn, president and chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh Asset Management. FED EXPECTED TO PAUSE ON RATES, FOR NOW Quarterly reports next week from chip companies Intel (INTC.O) and Sandisk (SNDK.O) also could influence the AI trade. Elsewhere, other high-profile companies set to report next week include drugmaker Eli Lilly (LLY.N) , oil majors Exxon (XOM.N) and Chevron (CVX.N) and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar (CAT.N) . The prospect for more interest rate hikes also comes into focus with the Fed meeting. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, in an effort to control above-target inflation, but Fed funds futures late on Friday suggested a less-than 10% chance the Fed will hike again when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, according to LSEG data. One factor: Investors are dubious that the Fed will want to increase rates just a week before the midterm elections. However, markets are leaning toward a hike at the next meeting in December, with futures suggesting a roughly 80% probability of such a move then. Walter Todd, chief investment officer at Greenwood Capital, said he will be watching for any hints about the rate path at Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference following the decision. "Does he say something to give an idea about December, because right now the expectation is there is going to be a hike," Todd said.

item.title: Ozempic wave boosts US cobblers and tailors as Americans tighten their belts
item.description: Read more in our series about weight-loss drugs and how they are changing our habits.
item.dc:creator: Danielle Kaye, Alexander Marrow
item.content:encoded: Lorraine Scott has spent at least $300 to tailor her pants and jeans since losing 60 pounds on weight-loss drugs over the past year. This is the fourth story in a five-part Reuters series on how weight-loss drugs are changing the way people shop and eat, and how companies are responding to the trend. "Most of the things in my closet didn't fit anymore," she said. The 42-year-old Atlanta resident, who is known as Lorraine Kamesha to her YouTube followers, has opted to alter her favorite pairs of pants instead of investing in new ones as her weight fluctuates, while turning to fast fashion for the rest of her wardrobe. US consumers taking weight-loss drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro have turned to cobblers and tailors as they try to save money while shedding pounds, motivated in part by a cost-of-living squeeze and rising out-of-pocket costs for the drugs as US employers [USN:L1N44L0V0 TEXT:"increasingly drop GLP-1 coverage"]. Over the past year, leather repairers have seen a spike in requests for their services due to rapid weight loss — not just for belts, but also for shoe and bag strap adjustments tailored to customers' trimmer bodies. The uptick in demand for alterations underscores how weight-loss drugs are upending the retail sector, with some corners of the industry well-positioned to benefit while others struggle to adapt. About 11% of US adults are on GLP-1 drugs to lose weight, according to Gallup, forcing millions of consumers to look for affordable ways to [USN:L6N43B0UY TEXT:"revamp their wardrobes"]. Cobblers Direct, an online shoe and handbag repair shop with 25 brick-and-mortar stores in Texas and a nationwide mail-in service, is seeing double-digit year-on-year growth in its belt-shortening business, said CEO Stephen Kelly. The company, whose around 100 artisans will soon be operating from a new, nearly 30,000-square-foot warehouse in Austin, is now shortening as much as 500 belts each week, Kelly said. Customers, he said, have been walking into the stores with five or six belts slung across their shoulder. After getting a few more holes punched in, some have asked to keep the extra flap of leather as a "badge of honor." "They'll pull their belt out and show how long their belt originally was. And then they tuck it back into their waistline," Kelly said. About 80% of GLP-1 users are living in clothes that no longer fit, waiting six months on average before buying anything new, according to a survey of more than 700 US adults using weight-loss drugs by telehealth platform Trimi. Jeans are the most disrupted article of clothing, the survey found, with 90% of users lamenting poor fit. After going off weight-loss drugs, people regain on average 60% of their lost weight within a year, researchers at the University of Cambridge found this year, adding to users' reluctance to go all-in on an entirely new wardrobe. At family-owned Jim's Cobbler Concierge in Manhattan, customers last year started bringing in belts by the dozens, said client relations director CJ Burgos — a trend so sweeping that the store has dubbed it "belt-zempic." GLP-1 users are even seeing their feet shrink, Burgos said, prompting an uptick in shoe adjustments. "It's helped the business, but we've also helped clients save," said Burgos, who has also brought in belts to shorten since losing about 60 pounds on Ozempic. SECONDHAND SEIZES THE MOMENT, TOO GLP-1 users are tightening their belts in more ways than one. The drugs' surging popularity in the US is also boosting discount chains, thrift shops and secondhand clothing platforms as many users refrain from splurging on new clothes while their size remains in flux. Compared to other business tailwinds, what sets GLP-1s apart is "the scale and speed," said Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at online thrift store ThredUp. Shoppers are shifting to smaller sizes, especially when buying jeans: 43% of buyers who started above a waist size 28 are now buying smaller jeans than when they joined ThredUp, Rotem said. Stitch Fix, an online personal styling service, is now offering more adjustable sizing and stretchy fabrics so that people who are rapidly losing weight have the "right apparel to help them bridge multiple sizes," said CEO Matt Baer. He estimated that at least 20% of the company's new clients are on a GLP-1 medication and looking for help finding new sizes. "We've always known that resale and thrift are very popular choices for people in life transition," said Rotem of ThredUp. "As we see that there are many more people in life transition with the advent of GLP-1s, we're leaning into that." item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La prix Nobel Maria Corina Machado est rentrée au Venezuela CARACAS, 25 octobre (Reuters) - La cheffe de file de l'opposition vénézuélienne, Maria Corina Machado, a annoncé dimanche être rentrée dans son pays après avoir passé près d'un an dans la clandestinité à l'étranger. Elections législatives en Serbie, l'opposition tente de renverser Vucic BELGRADE, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Serbes se rendent aux urnes dimanche alors que les opposants du dirigeant populiste Aleksandar Vucic, qui a accédé au pouvoir en 2014, l'accusent de corruption. Les Brésiliens aux urnes pour un second tour serré entre Lula et Bolsonaro SAO PAULO/RIO DE JANEIRO, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Brésiliens ont commencé à voter dimanche pour un second tour de la présidentielle qui s'annonce serré et qui pourrait faire basculer le plus grand pays d'Amérique latine vers la droite, comme nombre de pays de la région. Ouchakov, conseiller de Poutine, prône une implication européenne dans les efforts de paix en Ukraine MOSCOU, 25 octobre (Reuters) - L'Europe doit être impliquée dans les discussions sur une issue au conflit entre l'Ukraine et la Russie car sa position pourrait être déterminante, a déclaré dimanche Iouri Ouchakov, conseiller diplomatique du président russe Vladimir Poutine. L'Arabie saoudite intercepte des missiles et des drones 25 octobre (Reuters) - L'Arabie saoudite a intercepté dimanche des drones et des missiles au-dessus de sa capitale Ryad et du sud de son territoire, a dit la coalition emmenée par les Saoudiens contre les Houthis au Yémen. Russie-Trois morts dans des attaques dans la région de Belgorod MOSCOU, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Deux personnes ont été tuées et 13 autres blessées dans la nuit de samedi à dimanche par une attaque de drone ukrainienne contre la ville de Belgorod, en Russie, près de la frontière entre les deux pays, ont déclaré les autorités locales. Le séisme au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés Le séisme de magnitude 7 survenu au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés, a annoncé vendredi le gouvernement local sur les réseaux sociaux. Brésil-Lula et Bolsonaro mobilisent leurs partisans à la veille du second tour de la présidentielle SÃO PAULO, 24 octobre (Reuters) - Le président sortant Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva et le sénateur Flavio Bolsonaro ont clôturé samedi leur campagne en vue du second tour de l'élection présidentielle au Brésil, en mobilisant leurs partisans et en lançant un dernier appel aux électeurs indécis. Election présidentielle en Bulgarie dans un contexte d'attaques en mer Noire SOFIA, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Bulgares sont appelés aux urnes dimanche pour une élection présidentielle qui intervient alors que la guerre en Ukraine s'étend au large de la côte bulgare en mer Noire. Environ 1.200 Palestiniens déplacés à Hébron par une opération militaire israélienne JÉRUSALEM, 24 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée israélienne a contraint environ 1.200 Palestiniens à quitter leurs foyers à Hébron, en Cisjordanie occupée, a déclaré samedi un responsable palestinien, au lendemain d'une attaque qui a coûté la vie à deux soldats israéliens.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Marine Le Pen dit vouloir présider à la "Renaissance" de la France ORLEANS, Loiret, 25 octobre (Reuters) - La candidate du Rassemblement National (RN) à l'élection présidentielle de 2027, Marine Le Pen, a dit dimanche vouloir oeuvrer au "redressement" et même à la "renaissance" de la France, en combattant la résignation et le défaitisme qui prévalent selon elle dans le pays. Le suspect de l'attaque dans les Yvelines placé en observation psychiatrique PARIS, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Le suspect de l'attaque commise vendredi dans les Yvelines, qui a fait un mort et cinq blessés graves, dont une fillette de 12 ans, a été placé en observation psychiatrique, le temps d'apprécier si son état de santé est compatible avec la poursuite des auditions, a annoncé dimanche le parquet national antiterroriste (PNAT). La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque de Trappes prolongée La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque commise vendredi dans les Yvelines, qui a fait un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fillette de 12 ans, a été prolongée, a annoncé samedi le parquet national antiterroriste (PNAT). Jordan Bardella reconduit à la présidence du Rassemblement national Jordan Bardella a été reconduit samedi à la présidence du Rassemblement national, premier parti d'opposition de France, lors d'un congrès à Orléans (Loiret) où des personnalités de gauche ont participé de leur côté à une manifestation hostile à l'extrême droite. Veillée d'armes avant une nouvelle journée de manifestations, le dispositif sécuritaire renforcé La France se préparait vendredi à une nouvelle journée de manifestations à hauts risques samedi, une semaine après les violences et les pillages survenus en marge de défilés pour les conditions d'enseignement détériorées et contre la vie chère, obligeant l'exécutif à un sursaut. Le Pnat saisi après des tirs dans les Yvelines, sur place Macron dénonce un acte terroriste raciste Le président Emmanuel Macron s'est rendu à Trappes, dans les Yvelines, l'une des communes où un homme à bord d'un véhicule a tiré vendredi à l'arme automatique sur la voie publique, faisant un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fille de 12 ans. La tempête Austen balaie l'ouest de la France, 161.000 foyers privés d'électricité Quelque 161.000 foyers étaient privés d'électricité vendredi matin dans l'ouest de la France balayé par la tempête Austen, la première de l'automne, qui s'accompagne de vents violents, rapporte Enedis. Macron annonce l'interdiction des manifestations "sans légitimité" Les autorités interdiront dans les prochains jours les manifestations et regroupements sans "légitimité" et proposeront des "tracés alternatifs" aux syndicats pour protéger les centre-villes, a annoncé jeudi Emmanuel Macron, à deux jours d'un nouvel appel à manifester émanant notamment des "gilets jaunes". France: Premier décès lié au virus Shamonda, aucun risque sanitaire à ce jour selon les autorités Un patient est décédé début octobre du virus de Shamonda, une première en France et dans le monde, a annoncé jeudi le gouvernement, ajoutant qu'il n'y avait à ce stade aucun risque sanitaire pour la population générale au vu des connaissances sur ce virus. Cisjordanie: Les oliveraies de Palestiniens pillées lors d'attaques violentes de colons israéliens Ému aux larmes en se remémorant l'attaque contre son oliveraie par des colons israéliens il y a environ deux semaines près du village palestinien de Lubban al-Gharbi, en Cisjordanie, Ahmed Salem a déclaré s'être retrouvé impuissant, craignant d'être agressé s'il tentait d'intervenir pour protéger son exploitation.

item.content:encoded: Rallye-Le Dakar 2027 n'aura pas lieu en Arabie saoudite - organisateurs PARIS, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les organisateurs du Dakar ont annoncé dimanche que la 49e édition du célèbre rallye-raid, initialement prévu du 1er au 15 janvier, n'aurait pas lieu en Arabie saoudite en raison de la situation géopolitique dans le royaume. Football: Le match PSG-Lyon reporté à lundi La Ligue de football professionnel (LFP) a annoncé vendredi le report de dimanche à lundi de la rencontre entre le Paris Saint-Germain et Lyon, comptant pour la huitième journée de Ligue 1. Cyclisme: Le parcours du Tour de France 2027 Les organisateurs ont dévoilé jeudi le parcours du Tour de France 2027 : NFL: Rodgers soutient le choix de la ligue de maintenir le match en France malgré les manifestations Le quarterback des Pittsburgh Steelers Aaron Rodgers a défendu vendredi la décision de la National Football League (NFL) de maintenir la tenue du premier match de l'histoire de la ligue en France malgré un contexte social tendu à Paris. Football: La Confédération asiatique de football soutient finalement Infantino Le président de la Confédération asiatique de football (AFC), Cheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa, a annoncé vendredi le soutien de sa région à Gianni Infantino, candidat à sa réélection à la tête de la Fifa. Cyclisme: Les rouleurs à l'honneur du Tour de France 2027, le Puy de Dôme en conclusion du Tour Femmes Le Tour de France 2027, du 2 au 25 juillet, mettra à l'honneur les rouleurs avec un kilométrage contre-la-montre inédit depuis 2012, tandis que le Puy de Dôme sera l'épilogue du Tour de France Femmes, du 30 juillet au 7 août, ont dévoilé jeudi les organisateurs. Rallye: Le Dakar 2027 devrait faire son retour en Afrique - sources Le Dakar devrait faire son retour en Afrique pour sa 49e édition, en janvier prochain, en raison de la situation géopolitique au Moyen-Orient et en particulier en Arabie saoudite, où se déroule la course depuis 2020, ont indiqué à Reuters trois sources impliquées dans le championnat du monde de rallye-raid. Football: Roi des matches fous, le PSG assoit sa domination européenne En moins d'une semaine, le Paris Saint-Germain a battu sur un score identique Manchester City puis Barcelone (4-2), prouvant qu'il était bien, à l'heure actuelle, le favori à sa propre succession pour réaliser un rare triplé en Ligue des champions. Elina Svitolina annonce se séparer de Gaël Monfils, invoquant les conséquences de la guerre Elina Svitolina, sixième joueuse mondiale de tennis, a annoncé lundi se séparer du Français Gaël Monfils, ancien numéro six mondial du circuit ATP, l'Ukrainienne précisant que le poids émotionnel de la guerre menée par la Russie contre son pays natal l'avait amenée à ressentir le besoin de se redécouvrir. Voile-Barrier, première femme en solitaire sur un géant des mers Alexia Barrier paraît toute petite à la barre d'Idec Sport-CIC, un trimaran de 32 mètres capable de filer à plus de 40 nœuds. Bientôt, elle sera seule à bord.
